extracted.intended_audience: general readers and fans seeking a comprehensive biography of Ricky Gervais
extracted.subtask_description: Biographical encyclopedia entry summarizing Ricky Gervais's life, career, comedic style, influences, controversies, and works across film, television, radio, and other media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic style — observational satire
rubrics_metrics.description: "His comedy is observational and satirises everyday life."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This frames Gervais's primary comedic approach (examples in the page include The Office and Extras). It implies evaluation of material on whether it observes and satirises ordinary situations and social behaviour rather than relying on other comic modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit series length to preserve creative height
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision of John Cleese to stop making his acclaimed 1970s comedy sitcom Fawlty Towers after 12 episodes — when it was at its creative height — inspired Gervais in keeping his own sitcoms (The Office, Extras and Derek) to 12 episodes each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit production standard: intentionally capping series length (example: 12 episodes) to avoid creative decline. Use as a guideline when planning sitcom runs to preserve perceived quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provocation as a legitimate comedic tactic
rubrics_metrics.description: "You have to provoke. It's a good thing" (quoted in interview context).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page records Gervais's stated philosophy that provocation is part of comedy. Evaluation based on this metric considers whether material intentionally challenges or provokes audiences and whether that is judged artistically valuable, noting relevant high-profile examples (e.g., Golden Globes monologues) where provocation generated mixed reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use social media for promotion, fan engagement, and advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Gervais uses social media to promote his work to his fans... He also posts contests or questions to his fans as promotion for his series... Gervais uses social media to raise awareness of animal welfare. He tweets links to petitions... and he encourages people to adopt dogs instead of buying them from breeders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical standard for contemporary comedians: leverage platforms (Twitter, YouTube, etc.) to (a) promote projects (e.g., Learn Guitar with David Brent), (b) engage fans (contests/questions), and (c) pursue advocacy causes (animal welfare). The page cites awards and recognitions (Shorty Award, Genesis Award) as outcomes of effective social-media use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmedia/character-extension strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Gervais brought back his character Brent on his YouTube channel in a web series Learn Guitar with David Brent; performed the David Brent dance at live events and used the character to perform live gigs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A production/promotion approach: extending a popular character across media and live performance (TV, web, live gigs) to maintain audience interest and monetize/activate IP. The page gives examples of adapting the David Brent character for different contexts and platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and manage controversy when using edgy material
rubrics_metrics.description: Gervais has attracted criticism for the content of his stage routines and social media posts which have been called transphobic. Despite this, Gervais has stated that he supports trans rights, saying in his Netflix special “I support all human rights, and trans rights are human rights."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative dimension balancing intent, content, and public reaction: using provocative/edgy jokes can lead to accusations of prejudice; creators should expect scrutiny and may need to respond or clarify (examples: public criticism, awards despite controversy). This guidance captures both the reputational risk and the defensive framing recorded on the page.
